analysis.one_liner: Makes the IRS free Direct File tax-filing program permanent and nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The Get Your Money Back Act would require the IRS to keep operating Direct File, its free online system for preparing and submitting federal tax returns, and would require every state to take part starting after 2025. Today the program is voluntary for states and limited to 25 of them; this bill would make free direct filing available nationwide. Because it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and has seen no action since, it has not taken effect and nothing has changed.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers with simpler returns — especially working people who currently pay software companies or preparers to file — would be able to file their federal (and, once states join, state) returns directly with the IRS for free. The bill does not force anyone to use the system; it just keeps and expands the free option.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who pay to file

how_it_helps.text: It requires the IRS to keep running Direct File, the free system that lets taxpayers in participating states prepare and e-file federal returns at no cost through the IRS website.
For tax years after 2025, it requires all 50 states and DC to participate, extending free direct filing nationwide instead of the current 25 states.

analysis.who_pays: Tax preparation software companies and paid preparers would lose revenue from customers who switch to free government filing, and the Treasury would bear the ongoing cost of running a nationwide Direct File system.

drawbacks.text: The bill forces all states into the program by a fixed deadline, but Direct File today only handles relatively simple returns, so taxpayers with complex situations would still need paid software or a preparer.
The bill gives the IRS a permanent mandate without specifying new funding, so its cost to run a nationwide system falls on taxpayers through appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback is cost and design: a national Direct File program requires ongoing IRS funding and staff, and the bill does not say how it will be paid for; supporters of the current limited pilot also argue states and complicated situations (multi-state income, credits beyond the basic ones) are harder to handle. But the savings are real and direct for filers who now pay to file, and the free alternative — IRS Free File — is itself run through paid companies under contracts, so the free option's independence depends on government-run filing. On balance, the bill removes a recurring fee for a large number of Americans.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 30, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, or floor vote; the bill has sat in committee since referral.
It has only two cosponsors, both House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the paid tax-preparation industry is better off; it faces no new competition from a national free filing system, and taxpayers keep paying to file.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House members have taken a position (the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors); no Republicans have signed on, but no vote has occurred, so the partisan split is not yet known.

industries.industry: Tax preparation software companies (e.g., Intuit/TurboTax, H&R Block)
industries.note: Free government filing takes away paying customers, especially the simple-return filers these companies charge the most per dollar of value. Industry groups have lobbied against government-run filing for years.
Simple-return filers might file themselves for free instead of paying a preparer, though complex returns would still need professional help. The bill does not touch preparers directly.

analysis.trajectory: First bills like this rarely move unless leadership schedules action; with only two cosponsors and a referral to Ways and Means, the bill is likely to remain in committee and lapse at the end of the Congress unless it picks up significant support.
